School & learning

conjunction noun

also conjunctions, coordinating conjunction, coordinate conjunction, subordinating conjunction, subordinate conjunction, disjunctive conjunction, adversative conjunction, concessive conjunction, temporal conjunction, conditional conjunction

classical

Quint. 1.5.50: nam et an et aut conjūnctiōnēs sunt
Cic. Or. 135; Quint. 9.3.50 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 220, 235, 245
Lewis & Short s.v. conjūnctiō
Traupman 295

conjūnctiō, conjūnctiōnis f.

noun, third declension

a conjunction

In Cicero and Quintilian the connecting word of grammar, as well as any joining. The kinds are the later grammarians’: conjūnctiōnēs cōpulātīvae, coordinating (et, atque, ac), disjūnctīvae (aut, vel), adversātīvae (sed, at), with concessīvae, temporālēs and condiciōnālēs after them (Traupman 235–236, 246). Lewis & Short gives cōpulātīvus, disjūnctīvus, adversātīvus and concessīvus from late grammarians and Martianus Capella; Priscian’s adversātīvae were what we now call concessive (quamquam, etsī). Traupman calls a subordinating conjunction conjūnctiō subjūnctīva, as Charisius does (Lewis & Short s.v. subjūnctīvus).

Other words

  • convīnctiō, convīnctiōnis f. — a conjunction

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Quint. 1.4.18: in convīnctiōnibus autem complexūs eōrum esse jūdicāvērunt

    Quintilian’s preferred word, as the closer rendering of Greek σύνδεσμος, though he knows that most say conjūnctiō.

Examples

  • Dā conjūnctiōnēs cōpulātīvās.

    Give some coordinating conjunctions.Traupman 235

  • Conjūnctiō quid est?

    What is a conjunction?Traupman 235

  • conjūnctiō cōpulātīva

    a coordinating conjunctionTraupman 297
